questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: For which patient is intraosseous access indicated?
options: A critical patient who needs immediate vascular access
A stable patient with historically difficult veins
A patient who needs a second line for a second infusion
A patient refusing peripheral IV attempts
questions.explanation: There are only two indications for IO access: immediate vascular access in the critical patient, and cardiac arrest. Difficult venous access in a stable patient is not, by itself, a reason to drill.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: Which finding at or near the intended insertion site contraindicates IO placement?
options: A prosthetic implant in the opposite limb
A fracture of the intended insertion bone
An IO placed in the opposite limb 2 hours ago
A humeral site in a patient weighing 40 kg
questions.explanation: The three contraindications are a fracture of the intended insertion bone, a prosthetic implant at the insertion site, and recent IO access in the same limb. A prosthesis or a recent IO in the opposite limb does not bar the site you are using.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: An IO was placed in a patient's left tibia and has since been removed. Within what period is further IO access in that same limb contraindicated?
options: 6 hours
12 hours
24 hours
48 hours
questions.explanation: Recent (≤ 24 hours) IO access in the same limb is a contraindication, because extravasation from the earlier cortical breach makes infusate unreliable and risks compartment syndrome. The opposite limb remains available.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: At what patient weight is the EZ-IO 45 mm (yellow hub) needle used for a humeral head IO insertion?
options: > 15 kg
> 20 kg
≥ 40 kg
> 3 kg
questions.explanation: The humeral head carries more overlying soft tissue than the tibial sites, so in patients ≥ 40 kg the 45 mm yellow hub needle is needed to reach the medullary space. Too short a needle seats in soft tissue and the infusion infiltrates.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: With the IO needle tip resting on the bone before the trigger is squeezed, what confirms the needle is long enough?
options: The needle moves freely side to side
The stylet can be withdrawn without resistance
The hub sits flush against the skin
The 5-mm mark is visible above the skin
questions.explanation: The 5-mm mark is the most proximal mark to the hub; if it is still visible above the skin once the tip is on bone, there is enough needle left to cross the cortex. If it is not visible, a longer needle and/or a different insertion site is needed.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: What tells you to immediately release the EZ-IO driver trigger during insertion?
options: A sudden pop or loss of resistance
The hub contacts the skin
The driver's pitch changes
Blood appears at the needle hub
questions.explanation: The sudden pop or loss of resistance means you have entered the medullary space; continuing to drive risks passing through the far cortex. Placement is then confirmed by flushing the cannula with saline.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: The distal femur is permitted as an adult IO insertion site only in patients up to what age?
options: 8 years
12 years
13 years
21 years
questions.explanation: Adult sites are the proximal tibia, distal tibia and humeral head, with the distal femur allowed only if the patient is ≤ 21 years. Beyond that age the femoral marrow space is a poor target and the site is dropped.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: What minimum weight applies to the pediatric IO insertion sites?
options: > 3 kg
> 15 kg
> 20 kg
≥ 40 kg
questions.explanation: The pediatric sites — proximal tibia, distal tibia, humeral head and distal femur — apply to patients over 3 kg. Below that weight the bones are too small for the standard needle sets listed here.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: How is IO placement confirmed once the cannula is seated and the stylet removed?
options: Aspirate bone marrow into the syringe
Flush the cannula rapidly with saline
Attach a pressure bag and watch the drip chamber
Check for a waveform on the monitor
questions.explanation: Placement is confirmed by flushing the cannula with saline, and a rapid flush is specifically necessary before infusing anything, because it displaces the bone marrow that would otherwise obstruct flow. Patency must be reconfirmed before any medication or fluid.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: Flow through a correctly placed IO is inadequate for the volume you need. What should be done, and which site generally flows best?
options: Replace the needle with a longer one; the proximal tibia generally flows best
Place a second IO in the same limb; the distal femur generally flows best
Use a pressure bag or IV pump; the humeral head generally flows best
Use a pressure bag or IV pump; the distal tibia generally flows best
questions.explanation: IO flow is pressure dependent, so a pressure bag or IV pump is used when rates are inadequate, and the humeral head generally provides a higher flow rate than the other insertion sites.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: Where is the adult proximal tibia IO insertion site in relation to the tibial tuberosity?
options: Approximately 2 cm lateral to the tuberosity
Approximately 3 cm proximal to the tuberosity
Directly over the tuberosity
Approximately 2 cm medial to the tuberosity
questions.explanation: The adult proximal tibia site is about 2 cm medial to the tibial tuberosity, on the flat anterior surface. If the tuberosity cannot be palpated, the site is approximately 3 cm below the inferior border of the patella at that same level.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: Where is the adult distal tibia IO insertion site located?
options: Approximately 3 cm proximal to the medial malleolus
Approximately 3 cm proximal to the lateral malleolus
Directly over the most prominent part of the malleolus
Approximately 1 cm proximal to the medial malleolus
questions.explanation: The adult distal tibia site is roughly 3 cm proximal to the most prominent aspect of the medial malleolus, mid-line on the flat centre of the bone. The distal tibia usually has the least overlying tissue of any site.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: Where is the pediatric distal femur IO insertion site located?
options: 1-2 cm distal to the inferior border of the patella, in the mid-line
1-2 cm proximal to the superior border of the patella, about 1 cm medial to mid-line
3 cm proximal to the superior border of the patella, about 1 cm lateral to mid-line
Directly over the superior border of the patella
questions.explanation: With the leg outstretched so the knee cannot bend, the pediatric distal femur site sits roughly 1-2 cm proximal to the superior border of the patella and about 1 cm medial to the mid-line. Letting the knee flex moves the landmark.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: What must be achieved before a pediatric proximal humerus IO is attempted?
options: The deltoid insertion must be marked
The acromion must be palpable
The greater tubercle must be palpable
The arm must be abducted and externally rotated
questions.explanation: It is stated in red that you must be able to palpate the greater tubercle before insertion, to avoid errant placement. The arm is adducted and internally rotated — not abducted — to bring the tubercle up into the palm of your hand.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: What is the adult initial dose of 2% lidocaine for IO pain management?
options: 0.5 mg/kg
0.75 mg/kg
1 - 1.5 mg/kg
40 mg
questions.explanation: A conscious patient feels the infusate expanding the marrow cavity, so 40 mg of 2% lidocaine is given before flushing. The weight-based figures are the lidocaine doses used for arrest and tachycardia, not for IO analgesia.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: What is the pediatric initial dose of 2% lidocaine for IO pain management?
options: 0.5 mg/kg
0.75 mg/kg
1 - 1.5 mg/kg
40 mg
questions.explanation: The pediatric initial dose is 0.5 mg/kg, capped at the adult dose of 40 mg. It is given by the same route and timing as the adult dose: slowly, directly into the catheter hub, before the flush.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: What is the maximum initial dose of 2% lidocaine for pediatric IO pain management?
options: 3 mg/kg
4 mg/kg
20 mg
40 mg
questions.explanation: The pediatric 0.5 mg/kg dose is capped at 40 mg, which is the adult dose, so a larger child never receives more than an adult would. The mg/kg ceilings belong to lidocaine's arrest and local-anaesthesia indications.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: How is the initial dose of 2% lidocaine administered through an IO before the line is flushed?
options: Infuse over 60 seconds, then dwell 120 seconds
Infuse over 60 seconds, then flush immediately
Infuse over 120 seconds, then dwell 60 seconds
Infuse over 120 seconds, then flush immediately
questions.explanation: The lidocaine is infused slowly over 120 seconds and then allowed to dwell for 60 seconds so it can anaesthetise the marrow cavity before the normal saline flush drives it out. Flushing straight away wastes the dose and the flush still hurts.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: The patient still reports pain after the initial IO lidocaine dose. What repeat dose is given, and over what time?
options: Half the initial dose, infused over 60 seconds
Half the initial dose, infused over 120 seconds
The full initial dose, infused over 60 seconds
The full initial dose, infused over 120 seconds
questions.explanation: If additional lidocaine is needed after reassessment, half of the initial dose is given over 60 seconds — half the dose and half the infusion time of the first dose. For an adult that is 20 mg.

questions.title: Intraosseous Line Placement
questions.stem: Where is the lidocaine syringe attached when giving IO pain management?
options: To the primed EZ-Connect extension set
Directly to the IO catheter hub, without the extension set
To a stopcock between the extension set and the flush
To the side port of a pressure-bagged fluid line
questions.explanation: The syringe goes straight onto the catheter hub with no extension set, so the whole dose reaches the marrow rather than sitting in the dead space of the tubing. The primed extension set is attached afterwards and the line is then flushed.

questions.title: Invasive Hemodynamic Monitoring
questions.stem: To what pressure is the pressure bag inflated on an invasive hemodynamic monitoring set-up?
options: 100 mmHg
120 mmHg
150 mmHg
300 mmHg
questions.explanation: The bag is inflated to 300 mmHg, above any arterial pressure the patient can generate, so the flush device delivers its continuous low-rate flush and the catheter does not clot or back up. An underinflated bag is a classic cause of an over-dampened trace.

questions.title: Invasive Hemodynamic Monitoring
questions.stem: Where is the transducer placed and secured for invasive hemodynamic monitoring?
options: At the xiphoid process
At the mid-clavicular line, second intercostal space
At the phlebostatic axis
At the sternal angle
questions.explanation: The transducer is levelled and secured at the phlebostatic axis, the reference point for the right atrium. If it drifts above or below that level during transport, every pressure it reports is offset.

questions.title: Invasive Hemodynamic Monitoring
questions.stem: During invasive hemodynamic monitoring, what must be repeated with any change in altitude during transport?
options: Priming the transducer tubing
Replacing the dead-end caps
Re-inflating the pressure bag to 300 mmHg
Zeroing the transducer line
questions.explanation: Ambient pressure is the reference for the transducer, so a change in cabin altitude shifts the zero and every reading with it. The re-zero is built into the zeroing step rather than left to judgement.

questions.title: Invasive Hemodynamic Monitoring
questions.stem: When zeroing an invasive hemodynamic monitoring line, what is observed immediately after opening the stopcock to air?
options: A square waveform test
The IBP and NIBP difference
The pressure bag gauge
Return of the arterial waveform
questions.explanation: With the stopcock open to air, the square waveform test checks the dynamic response of the tubing and catheter before you press zero on the monitor. Comparing IBP with NIBP is the last step of the procedure, after the stopcock is returned.

questions.title: Invasive Hemodynamic Monitoring
questions.stem: For invasive hemodynamic monitoring, the sending facility's transducer is not compatible with LFN equipment. What should be done?
options: Use the existing line and zero it to the LFN monitor
Switch the line out and set up an LFN transducer
Monitor with NIBP alone for the transport
Contact medical control before transport
questions.explanation: An existing line may be used only when its transducer is compatible with LFN equipment; otherwise the line must be switched out and primed from step 3. An incompatible transducer cannot be reliably zeroed or read by the LFN monitor.

questions.title: Invasive Hemodynamic Monitoring
questions.stem: An arterial line waveform has become flat and over-dampened. Which check should be made?
options: Increase the monitor's sweep speed
Flush the catheter with a heparin syringe
Confirm no white caps remain in the set-up
Reposition the patient's arm and re-measure
questions.explanation: The over-dampened checklist is mechanical: air or kinks, pressure bag inflation, white caps left in place of dead-end caps, tubing disconnected from the patient, transducer position and waveform scale. A flat trace is far more often a set-up fault than a true loss of pressure.

questions.title: Invasive Hemodynamic Monitoring
questions.stem: Which port should be used to give medications to a patient with a pulmonary artery catheter?
options: The wedge balloon lumen
Any open stopcock on the transducer
The distal PA port
The right ventricular port
questions.explanation: Medications must not be infused through the distal PA port; the right ventricular port is used instead and may be capped and flushed. Drug delivered into the pulmonary artery bypasses mixing and the distal port is the pressure-monitoring lumen.

questions.title: Invasive Hemodynamic Monitoring
questions.stem: What is the guidance on obtaining a PCWP during transport of a patient with a pulmonary artery catheter?
options: There is no indication to wedge; document a PCWP before departure if available
Wedge only with medical control approval
Wedge the catheter once per hour and document the value
Wedge only if the distal waveform is dampened
questions.explanation: There is no transport indication for a PCWP, so the catheter should not be wedged — wedging risks pulmonary artery rupture and infarction. Any PCWP available from the sending unit is simply documented before departure.

questions.title: Invasive Hemodynamic Monitoring
questions.stem: Monitoring of a pulmonary artery catheter shows a PCWP tracing even though the wedge balloon is deflated. What should be done?
options: Flush the distal port and continue monitoring
Contact medical control for guidance
Withdraw the catheter until the PA waveform returns
Inflate and deflate the balloon to reposition the tip
questions.explanation: A spontaneous wedge means the catheter tip has migrated distally and the vessel is occluded, which risks infarction. Crews are not authorised to reposition the catheter; medical control is contacted.

questions.title: King Airway
questions.stem: Which patient meets the indication for a King airway?
options: Unconscious following a caustic ingestion
Unconscious with known esophageal disease
Unconscious with respiratory compromise and an absent gag reflex
Responsive with an intact gag reflex
questions.explanation: The single indication is an unconscious patient with respiratory compromise and an absent gag reflex. Caustic ingestion, known esophageal disease and a retained gag reflex are the three listed contraindications.

questions.title: King Airway
questions.stem: Which history contraindicates placing a King airway?
options: Suspected cervical spine injury
Recent oral surgery
Recent facial trauma
A caustic ingestion
questions.explanation: Caustic ingestion and known esophageal disease are contraindications because the distal cuff seats in an esophagus that may already be injured or friable. Suspected spinal injury is not a bar — the guideline simply directs maintaining spinal motion restriction instead of the sniffing position.

questions.title: King Airway
questions.stem: What determines which size KING LT(S)-D is selected?
options: The patient's weight or height
The patient's age
The width of the mouth opening
The distance from incisors to angle of the jaw
questions.explanation: Sizing is by weight or height, matching the manufacturer's colour-coded scheme. An undersized tube will not seal and an oversized one will not seat to the teeth.

questions.title: King Airway
questions.stem: How is the KING LT(S)-D introduced into the mouth, and when is it rotated?
options: Midline at 90°, rotated to the corner of the mouth once past the teeth
Into the corner of the mouth at 90°, rotated back to midline as the tip passes under the tongue
Midline along the hard palate, with no rotation
Into the corner of the mouth inverted, rotated 180° at the oropharynx
questions.explanation: The tube goes in at the corner of the mouth at a 90° angle and is rotated back to midline as the tip passes under the tongue, which sweeps the tongue out of the way and keeps the tip off the posterior pharyngeal wall.

questions.title: King Airway
questions.stem: How far is the KING LT(S)-D inserted?
options: Until resistance is met at the upper esophageal sphincter
To a depth of three times the tube's internal diameter
Until the flange of the connector aligns with the teeth
Until the proximal cuff is level with the lips
questions.explanation: The tube is advanced until the flange of the connector lines up with the teeth, and insertion must not be forced. Inflating the cuffs then lifts the device slightly as it seats.

questions.title: King Airway
questions.stem: What ETCO2 finding indicates appropriate ventilation through a King airway?
options: A rising value over three breaths
A sustained value above 30 mmHg
A value within 2-5 of the PCO2
A normal four-phase waveform
questions.explanation: ETCO2 must be attached to confirm placement and continuous monitoring maintained; a normal four-phase waveform is the sign that ventilation is reaching the lungs. Chest rise and bilateral breath sounds are assessed alongside it.

questions.title: King Airway
questions.stem: Ventilation cannot be accomplished through a newly placed King airway. What is the first corrective step?
options: Without deflating the cuff, pull back slightly and re-attempt ventilation
Add air to the cuffs and apply firmer downward pressure
Deflate the cuffs and advance the tube further
Withdraw the device completely and ventilate with a BVM
questions.explanation: The usual fault is the distal tip sitting too deep, so the first move is to pull back slightly with the cuffs still inflated and re-attempt. Only if that fails to seat the device is the cuff deflated and the tube slowly withdrawn and reassessed.

questions.title: King Airway
questions.stem: After the King airway cuffs are inflated, what is done with the inflation syringe?
options: Leave it attached to the inflation port
Place it to the right of the patient's head
Tape it to the tube at the level of the teeth
Discard it in the sharps container
questions.explanation: The syringe is not discarded; it is kept to the right of the patient's head so the cuffs can be deflated instantly if the device has to be repositioned or removed. Suction must also be available whenever the device is removed.

questions.title: Mandatory Use of ETCO2
questions.stem: For which airways is continuous ETCO2 monitoring mandatory?
options: Endotracheal tubes and surgical airways only
Any airway when the patient is being transported by air
All advanced airways, including ETT, SGA and surgical cricothyrotomy
Endotracheal tubes only
questions.explanation: Continuous ETCO2 is mandatory for every patient with an advanced airway — ETT, supraglottic airway or surgical cricothyrotomy — for the duration of transport. Its purpose is to catch unrecognised extubation and esophageal intubation.

questions.title: Mandatory Use of ETCO2
questions.stem: There is no consistent ETCO2 waveform on an intubated patient. What should be done?
options: Replace the ETCO2 sensor and continue ventilating
Auscultate the chest and epigastrium and continue if breath sounds are present
Increase the ventilation rate and reassess in one minute
Remove the ETT and ventilate by other means, or directly visualise the tube through the cords
questions.explanation: Without a consistent waveform the tube must be assumed misplaced: either remove it and ventilate by BVM, SGA or another intubation attempt, or prove placement by direct visualisation of the tube through the vocal cords. Breath sounds alone are not accepted as the substitute.

questions.title: Mandatory Use of ETCO2
questions.stem: Secretions and blood are interfering with ETCO2 measurement on an intubated patient. Which two options are sanctioned?
options: Remove the tube and provide effective BVM, or directly visualise the tube witnessed by another provider
Switch to colorimetric ETCO2, or document the absence of a waveform
Suction and accept the reading, or increase the ventilation rate
Remove the tube and place an SGA, or extubate and use high-flow oxygen
questions.explanation: When operational factors make the capnogram unreadable there are exactly two sanctioned options: remove the tube and ventilate effectively with a BVM, or have the tube's position directly visualised and witnessed by another LFN or EMS provider, using the CMAC's recording feature.

questions.title: Mandatory Use of ETCO2
questions.stem: Where is an HMEF placed when secretions, blood or vomit are fouling the capnography line on a patient with an advanced airway?
options: Immediately proximal to the oxygen source
Between the ETT/SGA and the ETCO2 sensor
Between the ETCO2 sensor and the BVM
On the expiratory limb of the ventilator circuit
questions.explanation: The HMEF sits between the airway device and the ETCO2 sensor, so it traps secretions before they reach the sensor. It is placed after effective airway suctioning, not instead of it.

questions.title: Mandatory Use of ETCO2
questions.stem: What should be considered to facilitate ventilation in a patient with an advanced airway?
options: A PEEP valve on the BVM
A second ETCO2 sensor on the expiratory limb
An OG tube to decompress the stomach
A nasopharyngeal airway alongside the ETT
questions.explanation: Gastric distension from pre-intubation bagging splints the diaphragm and worsens compliance, so an OG tube should be considered to decompress the stomach and make ventilation easier.

questions.title: Mechanical CPR Device
questions.stem: How should a STEMI or other critical patient who has not arrested be transported with respect to the mechanical CPR device?
options: On the AutoPulse running in continuous mode
On the AutoPulse in place with the LifeBand left open
Without a mechanical CPR device, which is applied only if arrest occurs
On the AutoPulse in place but powered OFF
questions.explanation: Critical non-arrest patients are preferentially transported with the AutoPulse already in place but powered off, so that if they decompensate there is no delay in starting compressions. Applying the device mid-arrest in a moving aircraft is the thing this avoids.

questions.title: Mechanical CPR Device
questions.stem: Where is the LUCAS suction cup positioned on the chest?
options: Over the lower half of the sternum, immediately above the xiphoid
Over the xiphoid process itself
At the inter-nipple line, centred on the left sternal border
Over the upper half of the sternum, below the manubrium
questions.explanation: The suction cup sits over the lower half of the sternum, immediately above the xiphoid. Too low compresses the xiphoid and abdominal organs; too high wastes force on the manubrium and generates no flow.

questions.title: Mechanical CPR Device
questions.stem: After pressing the LUCAS suction cup to the chest, what is done before compressions are started?
options: Draw a marker circle around the suction cup
Select PAUSE to lock the start position
Select CONTINUE to allow automatic sizing
Apply the stabilization strap
questions.explanation: PAUSE locks the LUCAS start position at the depth you have set, which is what makes the compressions reproducible; compressions are then begun in Continuous or 30:2 per protocol. The marker circle and stabilization strap come afterwards.

questions.title: Mechanical CPR Device
questions.stem: When is the LUCAS back plate slid beneath the patient, and to what level?
options: Once the patient is on the stretcher, to the level of the shoulders
Before manual CPR begins, to the level of the xiphoid
During the next planned rhythm check, to just below the axillae
After the first defibrillation, to the level of the iliac crests
questions.explanation: The back plate goes in during a rhythm check that was going to happen anyway, positioned below the axillae, so the only interruption in compressions is one that was already planned. Manual CPR continues the whole time the device is being prepared.

questions.title: Mechanical CPR Device
questions.stem: What anatomic landmark is aligned with the AutoPulse platform reference marks?
options: The patient's iliac crests
The patient's nipple line
The patient's xiphoid process
The patient's axillae
questions.explanation: The patient is transferred onto the platform with the axillae lined up to the reference marks and the torso centred, which puts the LifeBand across the correct part of the chest. A patient positioned too high or low on the platform compresses the wrong level.

questions.title: Mechanical CPR Device
questions.stem: Once the AutoPulse LifeBand is closed across the chest, which buttons are pressed and in what order?
options: CONTINUE, then START
PAUSE, then START
START, then the infinity sign
START, then CONTINUE
questions.explanation: CONTINUE lets the device perform its automatic sizing and calibration to the patient's chest, and only then does START begin compressions. Pressing START first would compress against an uncalibrated band.

questions.title: Mechanical CPR Device
questions.stem: Which AutoPulse indicator confirms the device is set to deliver continuous compressions?
options: The LifeBand tension indicator is green
The infinity sign button is lighted
The CONTINUE button is lighted
The battery indicator shows three bars
questions.explanation: The infinity sign button should be lighted to provide continuous compressions. If it is not, the device is cycling 30:2 rather than compressing continuously.

questions.title: Mechanical CPR Device
questions.stem: A mechanical CPR device alarms in flight and cannot be corrected immediately. What should be done?
options: Cycle the power and allow the self-test to complete
Continue the device and troubleshoot at the receiving facility
Immediately resume manual CPR
Pause compressions until the alarm is cleared
questions.explanation: A malfunctioning device is removed from the equation and manual CPR resumes immediately — on the AutoPulse that means taking the patient off the device. Troubleshooting never takes priority over perfusion.

questions.title: Mechanical CPR Device
questions.stem: Which event is an accepted reason to pause the mechanical CPR device during transport?
options: A scheduled battery change
Obtaining a 12-lead ECG
Repositioning the patient on the stretcher
Rhythm analysis
questions.explanation: Pauses are permitted only for rhythm analysis, pulse checks when indicated, defibrillation when indicated, or airway procedures when clinically necessary. Movement and routine tasks are done with the device running.

questions.title: Mechanical CPR Device
questions.stem: When a pause in mechanical CPR is necessary, what is the maximum interruption in compressions?
options: Less than 10 seconds
Less than 15 seconds
Less than 30 seconds
Less than 60 seconds
questions.explanation: Interruptions are kept as brief as possible with a maximum pause under 10 seconds, the same ceiling applied to device deployment. Coronary perfusion pressure falls away within seconds of stopping compressions and takes several compressions to rebuild.

questions.title: Mechanical CPR Device
questions.stem: What may crews see on ETCO2 while a mechanical CPR device is running?
options: Values higher than predicted because of the compression quality
Loss of waveform during the compression phase
Values that no longer correlate with perfusion
Values lower than predicted because of the fixed compression depth
questions.explanation: Continuous ETCO2 is used to verify compression quality, and the consistent high-quality compressions a device delivers often produce higher than predicted values. Knowing this prevents misreading a good number as ROSC.

questions.title: Mechanical CPR Device
questions.stem: What is the guidance on using mechanical CPR on a patient with an IABP, Impella or VAD?
options: It is permitted only with the LUCAS, not the AutoPulse
It may be used when indicated
It is absolutely contraindicated
It requires medical control approval first
questions.explanation: Mechanical CPR may be used in patients with cardiac assist devices when indicated; the contraindications table only directs caution, because positioning the patient on the device could migrate the catheter. Confirm device placement and securement before every move.

questions.title: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.stem: Which intubated patients must be transported on a mechanical ventilator?
options: Intubated patients with an expected transport over 30 minutes
Intubated patients who are not being hand-ventilated by a second crew member
All intubated patients, regardless of flight time
Intubated patients on flights longer than 15 minutes
questions.explanation: The Mechanical Ventilation guideline opens with a blanket statement: all intubated patients will be transported on a mechanical ventilator regardless of flight time. Hand ventilation does not deliver a consistent tidal volume or rate and is not an alternative for short legs.

questions.title: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.stem: Which ventilator mode is selected for a patient needing routine, standard lung protection?
options: ASV
PCV+
PSIMV+
APVcmv
questions.explanation: Routine lung protection uses APVcmv or APVsimv, because those modes let you set a target tidal volume and hold it as compliance changes. ASV is explicitly not approved for use at LFN.

questions.title: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.stem: Which ventilator mode is selected for a pediatric patient or a challenging adult with pulmonary disease or obesity, and why?
options: PCV+, because it sets a consistent PIP for patient safety
NIV-ST, because it adds a set respiratory rate
APVcmv, because it guarantees a target tidal volume
APVsimv, because it allows spontaneous breaths
questions.explanation: PCV+ or PSIMV+ are chosen for challenging mechanics because a pressure mode caps the PIP, protecting the lung when compliance or resistance is unpredictable. The trade-off is that tidal volume varies, so Vte must be watched.

questions.title: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.stem: What starting tidal volume is used in the basic ventilator settings?
options: 4 - 8 mL/kg
6 - 8 mL/kg
8 mL/kg
4 - 10 mL/kg
questions.explanation: Basic settings start at 6-8 mL/kg of ideal body weight, with Vte, Pplat and PIP monitored. The 4-8 mL/kg figure belongs to the severe hypoxia/ARDS strategy and 8 mL/kg to the pediatric/neonatal strategy.

questions.title: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.stem: What starting ventilator rate is set for an adult or a patient over 40 kg?
options: 15 BPM
17 BPM
20 BPM
25 BPM
questions.explanation: An adult or patient over 40 kg starts at 15 BPM with a permitted range of 8-25. The higher figures are the starting rates for the 30-40 kg, 20-30 kg and 10-20 kg weight bands.

questions.title: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.stem: What starting ventilator rate is set for a 7 kg infant?
options: 25 BPM
30 BPM
35 BPM
45 BPM
questions.explanation: A 7 kg patient falls in the 6-9 kg band, which starts at 30 BPM with a range of 20-40. Pediatric rates should start toward the lower end of the range because of the higher proportion of dead space, and Vt is increased before rate.

questions.title: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.stem: What starting inspiratory time is set on the ventilator for an adult?
options: 0.4 - 0.6 seconds
0.7 - 0.9 seconds
0.9 - 1.0 second
0.9 - 1.2 seconds
questions.explanation: The adult starting I-time is 0.9-1.0 second with a range of 0.7-1.2. The 0.9-1.2 figure is the pediatric value for age over 12 years, and the shorter times belong to younger children and infants.

questions.title: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.stem: What ventilator inspiratory time is set for a patient under 1 year of age?
options: 0.4 - 0.6 seconds
0.7 - 0.9 seconds
0.9 - 1.0 second
0.9 - 1.2 seconds
questions.explanation: Infants under 1 year get 0.4-0.6 seconds of inspiratory time; ages 1-12 get 0.7-0.9 and over 12 years get 0.9-1.2. Too long an I-time at an infant's rate leaves no time to exhale and causes air trapping.

questions.title: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.stem: What starting PEEP is used in the basic ventilator settings?
options: 3 cmH2O
5 cmH2O
10 cmH2O
15 cmH2O
questions.explanation: Basic settings start at 5 cmH2O with a permitted range of 3-20, titrated by watching Cstat, Pplat and driving pressure, and with caution in hypotension. 10 cmH2O is the ARDS starting point and 3 cmH2O the obstructive minimum.

questions.title: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.stem: Using the basic ventilator PEEP/FiO2 chart, what PEEP corresponds to an FiO2 of 60?
questions.explanation: The basic chart pairs FiO2 40 with PEEP 5, 50 with 8, 60 with 10, 70 with 10-14 and 80 with 15. Needing a high PEEP/FiO2 combination is the cue to move to the severe hypoxia strategy.

questions.title: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.stem: What ΔPcontrol does the Severe Hypoxia / ARDS ventilator strategy start at?
options: 10 cmH2O
15 cmH2O
25 cmH2O
27 cmH2O
questions.explanation: A Pcontrol of 15 over a PEEP of 10 sets the PIP at 25 with a driving pressure under 15, an ideal start for poorly compliant lungs that leaves room to raise either PEEP or Pcontrol. The 25 and 27 figures belong to the metabolic acidosis and obstructive strategies.

questions.title: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.stem: What adult rate does the Severe Hypoxia / ARDS ventilator strategy start at?
options: 10 BPM
15 BPM
24 BPM
32 BPM
questions.explanation: ARDS starts at 24 BPM in the adult, because a higher rate raises Pmean and compensates for the small tidal volumes compliance forces on you. The 10 and 32 figures are the obstructive and extreme metabolic acidosis rates.

questions.title: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.stem: What PEEP does the Severe Hypoxia / ARDS ventilator strategy start at, and in what increments is it then titrated?
options: A PEEP of 5 cmH2O, raised in 1-2 cmH2O increments
A PEEP of 10 cmH2O, raised in 1-2 cmH2O increments
A PEEP of 10 cmH2O, raised in 5 cmH2O increments
A PEEP of 15 cmH2O, raised in 1-2 cmH2O increments
questions.explanation: ARDS starts at a PEEP of 10 within a range of 3-20 and is raised in 1-2 cmH2O steps to find the optimal level. Stop raising it when Vte falls to unacceptable levels, driving pressure exceeds 15, or Cstat begins to fall.

questions.title: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.stem: On the ventilator, how is driving pressure calculated?
options: PIP minus PEEP
Pplat minus PIP
Pplat minus PEEP
Pmean minus PEEP
questions.explanation: Driving pressure is Pplat minus PEEP, equivalently Vte divided by Cstat. Keeping it under 15 is described as a method of minimising lung strain, and a driving pressure above 15 is one of the signals to stop raising PEEP.

questions.title: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.stem: What adult rate does the Obstructive / High Resistance ventilator strategy start at?
options: 10/min
15/min
24/min
32/min
questions.explanation: Obstructive patients start at 10/min, because a low rate buys the long expiratory time an asthmatic or COPD patient needs and the longer Ti needed to deliver a tidal volume against high resistance. Rates in the twenties stack breaths and cause air trapping.

questions.title: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.stem: What minimum PEEP is maintained in the Obstructive / High Resistance ventilator strategy?
options: 3 cmH2O
5 cmH2O
10 cmH2O
15 cmH2O
questions.explanation: Obstructive pathology already impedes exhalation and adding PEEP slows it further, so PEEP is dropped to a minimum of 3 and held there. With Pcontrol 27 over PEEP 3 the PIP sits at 30, the target starting point for these lungs.

questions.title: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.stem: What adult rate does the Extreme Metabolic Acidosis ventilator strategy start at?
options: 10/min
15/min
24/min
32/min
questions.explanation: Extreme metabolic acidosis starts at 32/min in the adult, because the patient was generating a large minute ventilation to compensate and dropping them to a normal rate will crash the pH. The goal is to return to a more routine strategy as the acidosis corrects.

questions.title: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.stem: When ventilating a patient in extreme metabolic acidosis, which formula determines the target PCO2?
options: PCO2 = (2 x HCO3) + 8 ± 2
PCO2 = (Vte / Cstat) + PEEP
questions.explanation: Winter's formula gives the PCO2 the patient must reach to maintain their compensation; ETCO2 generally runs 2-5 less than PCO2, so the number you aim for on the monitor is lower than the calculated target. (Vte / Cstat) + PEEP is the plateau pressure formula, not a PCO2 target.

questions.title: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.stem: What starting tidal volume does the Pediatric / Neonatal ventilator strategy set?
options: 4 - 8 mL/kg
6 - 8 mL/kg
8 mL/kg
10 mL/kg
questions.explanation: Pediatric and neonatal patients start at 8 mL/kg within a range of 4-10, deliberately higher than the adult start, because a slower rate with a larger Vt minimises the effect of their proportionally large dead space. Decrease it if PIP exceeds 30.

questions.title: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.stem: At what weight does the ventilator circuit switch from the neonatal T1 circuit to the adult/pedi T1 circuit?
options: 3 kg
15 kg
20 kg
40 kg
questions.explanation: The neonatal T1 circuit is used at or below 15 kg and the adult/pedi circuit above 15 kg. Using the larger circuit on a small child adds mechanical dead space, which is exactly what the pediatric strategy is trying to eliminate.

questions.title: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.stem: A ventilated child is hypercapnic. What should be increased first, and what changes that order?
options: Increase rate first; increase Vt once PIP reaches 30 cmH2O
Increase Vt first; increase rate once PIP reaches 30 cmH2O
Increase rate first; increase Vt once Pplat reaches 30 cmH2O
Increase I-time first; increase rate once PIP reaches 40 cmH2O
questions.explanation: In children, tidal volume is increased before rate because a larger breath dilutes the proportionally large dead space, while faster shallow breaths largely ventilate dead space. Only once PIP reaches 30 cmH2O does rate become the lever to pull.

questions.title: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.stem: A ventilated patient's Rinsp has risen into the red zone. What should be done?
options: Increase I-time and increase PEEP
Increase tidal volume and decrease rate
Decrease PEEP and increase FiO2
Decrease I-time and remove causative factors
questions.explanation: High inspiratory resistance is addressed by decreasing I-time and removing the causes — bronchospasm, a saturated HME, a small or kinked ETT, mucus. Medical control is contacted if PIP is sustained above 40.

questions.title: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.stem: What does a Low Oxygen alarm on the ventilator indicate?
options: Delivered FiO2 is more than 5% less than the set FiO2
The patient's SpO2 has fallen below the set alarm limit
The oxygen cylinder has less than 5% of its capacity remaining
The oxygen supply has failed completely
questions.explanation: Low Oxygen means the ventilator is delivering an FiO2 more than 5% below what was set, and it is distinct from 'Oxygen Supplied Failed'. A large minute volume or a large leak can outstrip the O2 plumbing, and the alarm can also mean an oxygen calibration is due.

questions.title: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.stem: A ventilator Pressure Limitation alarm is active. What is the first resolution listed?
options: Ensure adequate sedation and analgesia
Fix mechanical obstructions
Decrease Vt or Pcontrol
Increase the High Pressure Alarm limit
questions.explanation: The order matters: fix mechanical obstructions first — head of bed up to at least 45°, loosen seatbelts, remove the HME, suction, verify ETT placement — then sedation, then settings, and only last raise the alarm limit. Raising the limit first simply removes the warning without fixing the cause.

questions.title: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.stem: Where does the ventilator automatically set the Pressure Limitation line relative to the High-Pressure Alarm?
options: At the same value
At 5 cmH2O below it
At 10 cmH2O below it
At 15 cmH2O below it
questions.explanation: The Pressure Limitation line (blue) sits automatically 10 cmH2O below the High-Pressure Alarm line (red). It means the ventilator is capping pressure rather than reaching the alarm, which is why VTE can come in lower than expected.

questions.title: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.stem: What plateau pressure is targeted for most ventilated patients, and what is the allowance for an obese or rigid chest?
options: ≤ 25 for most patients, ≤ 30 if obese or rigid chest
≤ 30 for most patients, ≤ 35 if obese or rigid chest
≤ 30 for most patients, ≤ 40 if obese or rigid chest
≤ 35 for most patients, ≤ 40 if obese or rigid chest
questions.explanation: Target Pplat is ≤ 30 for most patients and ≤ 35 if the patient is obese or has a rigid chest, because much of the measured pressure in those patients is chest wall rather than alveolar. Plateau pressure can be calculated as (Vte / Cstat) + PEEP.

questions.title: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.stem: Beyond ETCO2, how many of the listed confirmation techniques are required to verify ETT placement?
options: At least three
All four
At least one
At least two
questions.explanation: In addition to ETCO2, at least two of the following are required: bilateral lung sounds with an absent epigastric sound, equal chest rise and fall, maintenance or increase in SpO2, and misting of the tube. No single one of these is reliable on its own.

questions.title: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.stem: Which ventilator mode is not approved for use?
options: ASV
PSIMV+
APVsimv
NIV-ST
questions.explanation: ASV is explicitly not approved for use. The approved modes are APVcmv and APVsimv for routine lung protection, PCV+ and PSIMV+ for challenging mechanics, and NIV/NIV-ST for non-invasive support.

questions.title: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.stem: On the LTV, which maneuver measures plateau pressure and what limits its availability?
options: An expiratory hold, available in any mode
An inspiratory hold, available only in volume mode
An expiratory hold, available only in volume mode
An inspiratory hold, available only in pressure mode
questions.explanation: Pplat is measured with an inspiratory hold, which the LTV offers only when in a volume mode. The expiratory hold is the separate maneuver used to measure AutoPEEP.

questions.title: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.stem: What bias flow is used for Low Pressure Oxygen on the LTV ventilator for adults and for pediatrics?
options: 5 LPM for adults and 10 LPM for pediatrics
10 LPM for adults and 5 LPM for pediatrics
15 LPM for adults and 5 LPM for pediatrics
20 LPM for adults and 10 LPM for pediatrics
questions.explanation: Low Pressure Oxygen uses a bias flow of 10 LPM for adults and 5 LPM for pediatrics, and the correct flow determines which of the two charts you read to set the input O2 flow against minute ventilation and desired FiO2.

questions.title: Mechanical Ventilation
questions.stem: Below what weight is pediatric tubing used on the LTV ventilator?
options: 3 kg
15 kg
20 kg
40 kg
questions.explanation: Pediatric tubing is used for patients weighing under 20 kg on the LTV. This is a separate threshold from the Hamilton circuit change, which happens at 15 kg.

questions.title: Needle Cricothyrotomy
questions.stem: In which patient is needle cricothyrotomy indicated rather than a surgical airway?
options: Any age, when a single intubation attempt has failed
Age under 8 years, as the first airway attempt in traumatic arrest
Age under 8 years, after less invasive airway methods have failed
Age under 13 years, when intubation is predicted to be difficult
questions.explanation: Needle cricothyrotomy is for the patient under 8 years in whom less invasive means of establishing an airway have already failed, together with failure to ventilate and oxygenate. It is a rescue, not a first attempt.

questions.title: Needle Cricothyrotomy
questions.stem: What is the listed contraindication to needle cricothyrotomy?
options: Inability to palpate the cricothyroid membrane
Age under 1 year
Suspected cervical spine injury
Ability to ventilate and oxygenate less invasively
questions.explanation: The only contraindication is that you can still ventilate and oxygenate some other way. An impalpable membrane is not a contraindication — it is addressed directly, since palpation is very difficult in infants and young children.

questions.title: Needle Cricothyrotomy
questions.stem: How is the cricothyroid membrane located for a needle cricothyrotomy?
options: By palpating the depression between the thyroid and cricoid cartilage
By palpating the depression between the cricoid cartilage and the first tracheal ring
By palpating the notch at the superior border of the thyroid cartilage
By measuring two finger-widths above the sternal notch
questions.explanation: The membrane is the palpable depression between the thyroid cartilage above and the cricoid cartilage below, and the neck is hyperextended first to bring it forward. That point is then stabilised between index finger and thumb for the puncture.

questions.title: Needle Cricothyrotomy
questions.stem: Immediately after puncturing the cricothyroid membrane, how is the needle's position in the trachea determined?
options: By attaching ETCO2 to the needle hub
By aspirating air with the attached syringe
By observing condensation in the catheter
By injecting 2-3 mL of sterile saline
questions.explanation: Aspiration of air with the syringe confirms the tip is in the trachea, and the metal needle must not be advanced any further once that is established. The same aspiration check is repeated after the metal needle is removed.

questions.title: Needle Cricothyrotomy
questions.stem: During needle cricothyrotomy, why must the metal needle not be advanced further once the catheter is being threaded?
options: It would kink the catheter
It would lacerate the thyroid cartilage
It would perforate the rear tracheal wall
It would transect the vocal cords
questions.explanation: Once in the trachea the needle is held still while the catheter is pushed forward along it, because advancing the metal needle would perforate the posterior tracheal wall. Held stationary, the needle serves as a guide and keeps the catheter from kinking.

questions.title: Needle Cricothyrotomy
questions.stem: When ventilating through a needle cricothyrotomy, what oxygen flow rate is set for the suction tubing and meconium aspirator set-up?
options: 5 LPM
10 LPM
20 LPM
questions.explanation: The oxygen source is set to 12-15 LPM, and insufflation is produced by occluding the hole on the mask/ETCO2 adaptor and the hole on the meconium aspirator simultaneously until chest rise is seen.

questions.title: Needle Cricothyrotomy
questions.stem: What I:E ratio is used for ventilating through a needle cricothyrotomy?
options: Approximately 1:1
Approximately 1:2
Approximately 1:4
Approximately 3:1
questions.explanation: Ventilation uses roughly 1:4, a long expiratory time, because exhalation through a narrow catheter and a partially obstructed upper airway is slow. The ETCO2 waveform is watched back to baseline to confirm full exhalation before the next breath.

questions.title: Needle Cricothyrotomy
questions.stem: Which three findings confirm placement after a needle cricothyrotomy?
options: ETCO2, aspiration of air and chest rise
Breath sounds, chest rise and absence of subcutaneous emphysema
Aspiration of air, misting of the catheter and an increase in SpO2
ETCO2, breath sounds and an increase in SpO2
questions.explanation: Confirmation is ETCO2, breath sounds and a rise in SpO2 together. ETCO2 readings through a needle airway may be inaccurate but will still be present with accurate placement, so the waveform's presence matters more than its number.

questions.title: Needle Cricothyrotomy
questions.stem: What is the key to success when performing a needle cricothyrotomy on an infant or young child?
options: Immobilisation of the trachea throughout the procedure
Using the smallest available catheter
Hyperextending the neck over a shoulder roll
Having a second provider ventilate throughout
questions.explanation: The infant larynx is small, soft and mobile, so the membrane slides away from the needle unless the trachea is held still throughout. Immobilisation of the trachea is named as the key to success.

questions.title: Needle Cricothyrotomy
questions.stem: During a needle cricothyrotomy, all attempts to place the needle have failed and the child cannot be oxygenated. What is permitted next?
options: Place a supraglottic airway and transport
Incise the skin over the membrane and dissect until it is visible
Perform a surgical cricothyrotomy with a bougie and 6.0 ETT
Attempt the puncture one rib space lower over the trachea
questions.explanation: When the membrane cannot be palpated and the patient cannot be oxygenated, the crew may incise the skin over the area and gently dissect until the membrane is visible, then place the needle through it as described. This is an aid to seeing the membrane, not a conversion to a surgical airway.

questions.title: Needle Cricothyrotomy
questions.stem: A needle cricothyrotomy is found to have been incorrectly placed. What is required?
options: Document the finding in the PCR at the end of the shift
Notify the receiving physician and note it in the transfer report
Immediately notify the CMOC and submit a QM report
Notify the base manager within 24 hours
questions.explanation: Incorrect placement triggers immediate CMOC notification and a QM report. Separately, the name of the receiving provider who confirmed placement on transfer of care must be documented in the PCR for every needle cricothyrotomy.

questions.title: Needle Thoracostomy
questions.stem: Which finding is REQUIRED to be present before performing a needle thoracostomy?
options: Tracheal deviation
Jugular venous distention
Decreased breath sounds
Hypotension
questions.explanation: Hypotension must be present to perform a needle thoracostomy, as stated in red; the other findings — tachycardia, decreased breath sounds, JVD, hypoxia, hypocarbia, tracheal deviation — are supporting signs that accompany it. Traumatic arrest is the separate standalone indication.

questions.title: Needle Thoracostomy
questions.stem: What is the listed contraindication to needle thoracostomy?
options: A pneumothorax without tension physiology
A chest tube already in place on that side
Bilateral decreased breath sounds
Penetrating trauma to the affected hemithorax
questions.explanation: A simple pneumothorax without tension physiology is the contraindication, because decompressing it converts a stable injury into an open communication with the pleural space for no haemodynamic benefit. Tension physiology, with hypotension, is what justifies the needle.

questions.title: Needle Thoracostomy
questions.stem: Where is the anterior needle thoracostomy site located?
options: 2nd intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line
2nd intercostal space at the anterior axillary line
3rd intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line
4th intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line
questions.explanation: The anterior site is the 2nd intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line. The 2nd rib is found where it attaches to the sternum at the manubriosternal junction, the Angle of Louis, and the space below it is the target.

questions.title: Needle Thoracostomy
questions.stem: Where is the lateral needle thoracostomy site located?
options: 2nd or 3rd intercostal space, between the anterior and mid-axillary line
4th or 5th intercostal space, between the anterior and mid-axillary line
5th or 6th intercostal space, posterior to the mid-axillary line
4th or 5th intercostal space, medial to the nipple line
questions.explanation: The lateral site is the 4th or 5th intercostal space, lateral to the nipple or inframammary crease, between the anterior and mid-axillary line. If the level is hard to judge, err to the next rib level superior.

questions.title: Needle Thoracostomy
questions.stem: During needle thoracostomy, how is the needle advanced in relation to the rib?
options: Contact the inferior aspect of the rib and advance through the intercostal muscle
Walk the needle off the inferior aspect of the rib and advance below it
Contact the superior aspect of the rib, withdraw slightly, then advance just above it
Advance through the middle of the intercostal space without seeking the rib
questions.explanation: You deliberately contact the superior aspect of the rib to gauge depth, note that depth at skin level, then withdraw slightly and pass just above the rib. Passing above the rib keeps the needle away from the neurovascular bundle running along the rib's inferior margin.

questions.title: Needle Thoracostomy
questions.stem: Which findings tell you the needle has entered the pleural space during a needle thoracostomy?
options: Blood return into the catheter hub
Loss of the ETCO2 waveform
Immediate return of breath sounds on that side
A pop, decreased resistance, or a rush of air
questions.explanation: The pop, the drop in resistance and the rush of air as tension is relieved are what signal entry into the pleural space. The needle is then stabilised and the catheter threaded in before the needle is removed and a one-way valve placed.

questions.title: Needle Thoracostomy
questions.stem: During needle thoracostomy, the catheter will not thread off the needle. How far beyond the depth measured at rib contact may you insert before reassessing landmarks and placement?
options: 1 cm
2 cm
3 cm
5 cm
questions.explanation: If the needle has gone 3 cm beyond the depth noted when rib contact was made and the catheter still will not thread, you are almost certainly not in the pleural space, so landmarks and placement are reassessed rather than pushing deeper.

questions.title: Needle Thoracostomy
questions.stem: Tension physiology recurs after a successful needle thoracostomy. What should be done?
options: Repeat the needle decompression or perform a finger thoracostomy
Remove the one-way valve and leave the catheter open to air
Increase PEEP and transport without further intervention
Aspirate the existing catheter with a syringe
questions.explanation: Catheters kink, clot and fall out of the pleural space, so recurrent tension is treated by repeating the decompression or escalating to a finger thoracostomy. The recurrence itself is evidence the first catheter is no longer working.

questions.title: Needle Thoracostomy
questions.stem: Which device is used for needle thoracostomy in infants and small children?
options: A jet ventilation catheter
A 16- or 18-gauge IV catheter
A 10-gauge 3.25 inch Enhanced ARS needle
A 22-gauge IV catheter
questions.explanation: Infants and small children get a 16- or 18-gauge IV catheter; the 10-gauge 3.25 inch Enhanced ARS needle used in larger patients is far longer than the chest wall depth of a small child and risks injuring lung or mediastinal structures.

questions.title: Needle Thoracostomy
questions.stem: When performing needle thoracostomy at the lateral site, in what direction is the catheter threaded?
options: Toward the diaphragm
Straight in, perpendicular to the chest wall
Toward the middle of the clavicle
Toward the sternal notch
questions.explanation: At the lateral site the catheter is advanced toward the middle of the clavicle, which directs it into the apex of the pleural cavity where air collects in a supine patient. The needle is held stationary while the catheter advances off it.

questions.title: Non-Invasive Ventilation (CPAP & BiPAP)
questions.stem: Which patient meets an indication for non-invasive ventilation?
options: A trauma patient with a flail chest and hypoxia
A patient with severe altered level of consciousness
A patient with a known pneumothorax and hypoxia
A medical patient in moderate to severe respiratory distress
questions.explanation: NIV is indicated for medical patients in moderate to severe respiratory distress, CHF/pulmonary edema, asthma/COPD, and pre-oxygenation for RSI. Severe altered LOC and pneumothorax are listed contraindications.

questions.title: Non-Invasive Ventilation (CPAP & BiPAP)
questions.stem: Below what systolic blood pressure is non-invasive ventilation contraindicated?
options: SBP < 80
SBP < 90
SBP < 100
SBP < 110
questions.explanation: NIV is contraindicated below an SBP of 100, because the positive intrathoracic pressure reduces venous return and will drop the pressure further in a patient with no reserve. The other contraindications are severe altered LOC, inability to maintain the airway, and pneumothorax.

questions.title: Non-Invasive Ventilation (CPAP & BiPAP)
questions.stem: What type of mask is required for NIV, including when a mask is taken from the sending hospital?
options: A non-vented mask
A vented mask
A non-rebreather mask with a reservoir
A mask with an integral exhalation port
questions.explanation: NIV delivered by a mechanical ventilator requires a non-vented mask, and it is highlighted in red that any mask borrowed from the hospital must be checked to be non-vented. A vented mask dumps the circuit pressure and the ventilator cannot support the patient.

questions.title: Non-Invasive Ventilation (CPAP & BiPAP)
questions.stem: What initial Psupport (IPAP) is set when starting CPAP on the ventilator?
options: 0 cmH2O
2 cmH2O
5 cmH2O
10 cmH2O
questions.explanation: CPAP by definition adds no inspiratory support above the baseline, so Psupport is set to 0 with a PEEP (EPAP) of 5. BiPAP is the same table with Psupport set to 5.

questions.title: Non-Invasive Ventilation (CPAP & BiPAP)
questions.stem: What initial Psupport (IPAP) and PEEP (EPAP) are set when starting BiPAP on the ventilator?
options: Psupport 0, PEEP 5
Psupport 5, PEEP 5
Psupport 5, PEEP 10
Psupport 10, PEEP 5
questions.explanation: BiPAP starts at Psupport 5 over PEEP 5, with FiO2 patient dependent, and on the LTV a Rise Time of 2 and Flow Term of 40%. Both pressures are then titrated to the patient's presentation.

questions.title: Non-Invasive Ventilation (CPAP & BiPAP)
questions.stem: What difference should be maintained between Psupport and PEEP while titrating NIV?
options: 2 - 3 cmH2O
4 - 5 cmH2O
6 - 8 cmH2O
8 - 10 cmH2O
questions.explanation: A 4-5 cmH2O gap between Psupport and PEEP is maintained as both are titrated, so the patient keeps a meaningful pressure support breath rather than having the two values converge into plain CPAP.

questions.title: Non-Invasive Ventilation (CPAP & BiPAP)
questions.stem: When is the NIV mask placed on the patient relative to starting the ventilator?
options: Before the ventilator is started, so the seal can be checked
At the same time as the ventilator is started
After the ventilator has run for several breaths
After the patient has been coached through three practice breaths
questions.explanation: Mask and ventilator start together: applying the mask first is uncomfortable for a breathless patient, and starting the ventilator first produces low pressure alarms into an open circuit. The mask is then strapped and the Leak% checked.

questions.title: Non-Invasive Ventilation (CPAP & BiPAP)
questions.stem: A patient on NIV says "I'm not getting enough air." Which adjustments should be made?
options: Shorten the P-ramp, decrease Psupport, increase ETS% and Ti Max
Lengthen the P-ramp, increase Psupport, increase ETS% and Ti Max
Shorten the P-ramp, increase Psupport, decrease ETS% and Ti Max
Lengthen the P-ramp, decrease Psupport, increase ETS% and Ti Max
questions.explanation: Shortening the P-ramp delivers the breath faster, raising Psupport delivers more of it, and lowering ETS% and Ti Max lets inspiration run longer before cycling. The opposite set of moves is the answer when the patient says it is too much air.

questions.title: Non-Invasive Ventilation (CPAP & BiPAP)
questions.stem: A patient on NIV says "It's forcing air, I can't breathe out." What adjustment should be made?
options: Decrease ETS% (Flow Term) and Ti Max
Increase Psupport and shorten the P-ramp
Decrease PEEP and increase FiO2
Increase ETS% (Flow Term) and Ti Max
questions.explanation: Raising ETS% makes the ventilator cycle into exhalation at a higher fraction of peak flow, ending inspiration sooner, and Ti Max caps how long a breath can last. That is the specific fix when the patient cannot get out of the breath.

questions.title: Non-Invasive Ventilation (CPAP & BiPAP)
questions.stem: VTE is rising on a patient receiving NIV. What does this indicate, and what should be done?
options: The patient's condition improving; decrease Psupport
A developing leak; check the mask seal
Low patient effort; increase Psupport
Progression to respiratory failure; prepare for intubation
questions.explanation: A rising VTE means the patient is moving more air and is getting better, so the support is weaned by decreasing Psupport. Falling VTE is the worrying direction — leak, low patient effort, or progression to respiratory failure.

questions.title: Non-Invasive Ventilation (CPAP & BiPAP)
questions.stem: A patient remains intolerant of NIV after the P-ramp and ETS% have been adjusted. Which agents are preferred for light sedation?
options: Low dose haloperidol or droperidol
Low dose fentanyl or ketamine
Low dose midazolam or lorazepam
Low dose propofol or etomidate
questions.explanation: Low dose fentanyl or ketamine are preferred, and it is stated in red that benzodiazepines should be avoided because their effects are unpredictable and may decrease mental status — which would then contraindicate the NIV. Settings must be adjusted before any drug is given.

questions.title: Non-Invasive Ventilation (CPAP & BiPAP)
questions.stem: A Hamilton ventilator is set to 10/5 for NIV. What are the underlying Psupport and PEEP values?
options: Psupport 10 and PEEP 10
Psupport 10 and PEEP 5
Psupport 5 and PEEP 5
Psupport 15 and PEEP 5
questions.explanation: On the Hamilton, IPAP and EPAP are additive: a displayed 10/5 is a Psupport of 5 sitting on top of a PEEP of 5. Reading it as a Psupport of 10 would mean delivering twice the intended support.

questions.title: Non-Invasive Ventilation (CPAP & BiPAP)
questions.stem: A CHF patient on NIV needs nitroglycerin. What should be done?
options: Give nitroglycerin paste and continue NIV
Withhold nitroglycerin until NIV is discontinued
Remove the mask briefly to give nitroglycerin tabs
Initiate a nitroglycerin infusion rather than removing the mask
questions.explanation: An infusion avoids interrupting the positive pressure that is recruiting alveoli and offloading the failing ventricle, which is the whole point of the mask. Taking the mask off a pulmonary edema patient to place a tab under the tongue undoes that in seconds.

questions.title: Pelvic Binder
questions.stem: Which patient meets an indication for a pelvic binder?
options: A mechanism consistent with pelvic fracture and shock with no other obvious source of hemorrhage
Any high-speed motor vehicle collision, regardless of findings
Pelvic pain on palpation with a normal blood pressure
Hemorrhagic shock with a femur fracture and an obvious thigh hematoma
questions.explanation: The indications are a known or suspected unstable pelvic fracture, a mechanism consistent with pelvic fracture and/or hemorrhagic shock without another obvious source of hemorrhage, and traumatic arrest. If the bleeding source is obvious elsewhere, the binder is not what the patient needs.

questions.title: Pelvic Binder
questions.stem: Below what age is a pelvic binder not recommended?
options: 8 years
10 years
13 years
18 years
questions.explanation: There are no absolute contraindications, but the binder is not recommended under age 13, largely because the SAM sling sizes start at a hip circumference of 27 inches and will not sit correctly on a smaller pelvis.

questions.title: Pelvic Binder
questions.stem: How is the SAM pelvic sling oriented and positioned when placed beneath the patient?
options: Black side up, at the level of the umbilicus
Grey side up, at the level of the hips
Grey side down, at the level of the hips
Grey side up, at the level of the iliac crests
questions.explanation: The sling goes grey side up, beneath the patient at the level of the hips, so the buckle mechanism faces outward and compression is applied across the greater trochanters rather than the iliac crests. Pockets must be emptied and, in males, the genitalia elevated out of the groin first.

questions.title: Pelvic Binder
questions.stem: How is tension applied to the SAM pelvic sling, and what tells you it is correct?
options: Pull the black strap through the buckle until hand-tight, then tape it down
Pull both straps evenly until the patient reports relief of pain
Hold the orange strap and pull the black strap the opposite way until the buckle clicks
Hold the black strap and pull the orange strap until the straps overlap by 6 inches
questions.explanation: After passing the black strap completely through the buckle, you hold the orange strap and pull the black strap in the opposite direction until you both feel and hear the buckle click, which is the device's built-in indicator of correct tension. Tension is then maintained while the black strap is pressed onto the splint surface.

questions.title: Pelvic Binder
questions.stem: Immediately after the SAM pelvic sling buckle clicks, what should be done?
options: Reassess the pelvis before securing the strap
Add a second sling above the first for additional compression
Release tension slowly and check distal pulses
Maintain tension and press the black strap onto the splint surface
questions.explanation: Tension is held while the black strap is pressed down onto the surface of the SAM splint, which is what locks the compression in; letting go first lets the sling loosen before it is secured. Reassessment follows once the binder is secured.

questions.title: Pelvic Binder
questions.stem: When preparing the pelvic area of a male patient for a pelvic binder, what should be done?
options: Ensure the genitalia are elevated out of the groin area
Apply a protective pad over the groin before the sling
Place the sling higher, above the iliac crests
Leave clothing in place to protect the skin
questions.explanation: Objects are removed from the pockets and pelvic area and the genitalia are lifted clear of the groin, because the sling applies sustained circumferential compression and anything trapped under it will be injured over the course of the transport.

questions.title: Pelvic Binder
questions.stem: After a pelvic binder is applied, how often are the pelvic area, distal circulation, sensation and motor function reassessed?
options: Every 5 minutes
Every 10 minutes
Every 15 minutes
Every 30 minutes
questions.explanation: Distal circulation, sensation and motor function are reassessed every 15 minutes and the findings documented in the PCR, because a binder tight enough to close the pelvic ring can also compromise the limbs. The same assessment is performed before application as a baseline.
